analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to cover workers and families under health insurance or pay a tax, with a new public plan for everyone else.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees and four subcommittees in 1993, never received a markup or a floor vote, and died when the 103rd Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required every employer to enroll its employees and their families in a certified health plan, with employers picking up most of the premium; small employers could instead buy into a new Medicare-style public health plan that anyone without other coverage could join. It set annual caps on national health spending, created a federal commission and state commissions to set provider payment rates, barred insurers from rejecting people for pre-existing conditions or charging sick people more, and added preventive screenings to Medicare. It paid for the public plan with a new tax on employers who did not cover workers, the full amount of Medicare payroll taxes above the current wage cap, and new tax deductions for self-employed people and small employers.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and their families would gain guaranteed coverage through their employer with limits on employee premiums (capped at 20 percent of the plan's cost) and out-of-pocket costs, protection against being denied coverage for health status, and at most a six-month pre-existing-condition exclusion that would phase out for basic services [S2][S3]. People without job-based coverage — the self-employed, unemployed, part-time and seasonal workers — could enroll in the new public health plan with benefits modeled on Medicare, and people below the poverty line could get help eliminating their cost-sharing [S2]. Medicare beneficiaries would gain coverage for colorectal and breast cancer screening, flu and tetanus shots, and well-child care [S2]. Small employers would gain a 20 percent deduction for premiums and the option to buy coverage through the public plan [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Employers who fail to cover an employee and dependents face a $100-per-day excise tax, phased in from January 1994 for the largest employers down to small employers by 1997 [S3].

A Medicare-style public health plan would be open to any U.S. citizen or legal resident not covered by Medicare, an employer plan, or a federal plan, with a $250 individual ($500 family) deductible, a $2,500 annual out-of-pocket cap, no cost-sharing for preventive services, and low-income assistance that limits or eliminates cost-sharing below the poverty line [S2][S3].

Insurers could not deny or price group coverage based on health status, claims experience, or medical history; small-employer plans must be community-rated, guaranteed-issue, continuously renewable, and at least 12 months long [S2].

National health spending caps, a Federal Health Care Cost Containment Commission, and state commissions would set provider payment rates used by Medicare, the public plan, and qualified private plans, and a global fee with a 5 percent surcharge on cesarean sections targets a costly procedure [S2].
Medicare payroll tax contributions would no longer stop at the annual wage cap, making the financing of hospital insurance progressively funded [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers would bear the main cost: the $100-per-day tax for uncovered workers and the bulk of premiums in qualified plans, with employee premiums capped at 20 percent of the plan's cost [S2][S3]. High-earning workers would pay more through the removal of the wage cap on the hospital insurance tax [S2]. Health insurers and health care providers would face certified-plan standards, community rating, spending caps, and commission-approved payment rates [S2].

drawbacks.text: Employers would face a $100-per-day tax per uncovered employee and would fund most premiums; the requirement applies to part-time employees on the same terms as full-time, and employee premiums are capped at 20 percent of the plan's cost, so the employer share is large [S3].

The bill imposes national annual limits on health care spending, apportioned among states and among classes of providers by government commissions, which critics of such global budgeting argued could restrict access to care and was the centerpiece of 1990s managed-competition objections [S2].

It repeals COBRA continuation coverage (the right to keep employer coverage temporarily after job loss) on the theory that the new public plan would catch people who lose coverage, but coverage gaps could result during the multi-year phase-in, when full enrollment requirements do not reach small employers until 1997 [S2][S3].

After a transition period, individuals not enrolled in a plan would be deemed enrolled in the public plan and could owe twice the premiums they would have paid if enrolled on time, and the bill preempts state benefit-mandate laws, overriding state coverage requirements [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary people the potential gains were large: near-universal coverage, limits on premiums and out-of-pocket costs, an end to health-status discrimination, and national cost containment. The costs fell mainly on employers and upper-income households through taxes, and the design carried real risks — global spending caps set by commission could ration care, COBRA repeal created transition-period gaps, and an individual enrollment mandate enforced through tax returns could hit people who fell through the cracks. It was one of the more ambitious employer-mandate-plus-public-option proposals of 1993, with stronger cost controls than most rivals but a longer and more disruptive phase-in.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and split among four subcommittees, none of which acted, and its last action was an August 1993 cross-reference to another bill before the 103rd Congress ended without a vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Benjamin Cardin introduced the bill on March 18, 1993, with no cosponsors [S1][S4][S5].
The House referred it jointly to the Committees on Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and Labor [S5].
In April 1993 it was referred to four subcommittees: Health (Ways and Means), Labor-Management Relations, Commerce, Consumer Protection and Competitiveness, and Health and the Environment [S5].
No subcommittee or full committee held a markup, and the bill never reached the House floor [S5].
Its final action, on August 10, 1993, was a cross-reference to H.R. 2264, and the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 with no further action [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers avoided a coverage mandate, a public-plan competitor, and commission-set payment rates. The 40 million or so uninsured Americans of the era — many of them working people — gained nothing; the 103rd Congress ended without any comprehensive health reform becoming law.

for.name: Rep. Benjamin Cardin (D-MD)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 18, 1993 and delivered introductory remarks; it was his only support on the record, as no member cosponsored it

against.name: Chairmen of the three committees of referral
against.role: Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in March 1993, sent it to subcommittees, and never reported it or held a markup during the 103rd Congress

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Focused the 1993-94 health reform debate on the leadership's own bill (H.R. 3600, the Health Security Act) and never scheduled this proposal for floor action

against.name: Health insurance industry
against.what_they_did: Ran a well-funded national advertising and lobbying campaign in 1993-94 against employer-mandate and government-plan health reform proposals of this type

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill had a single Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and died in committees controlled by the same party, so its partisan shape cannot be measured.

industries.note: The employer mandate would force millions of workers into certified private plans, but the bill also channels small employers and the uninsured into a competing public plan and subjects insurers to community rating, guaranteed issue, standard benefit packages, and commission-set payment rates. Insurers' interest in avoiding those rules ran against the uninsured workers the bill would cover.

industries.industry: Employers, especially mid-size and large businesses
industries.note: Employers would owe a $100-per-day tax per uncovered worker and pay most of the premium for employee and family coverage. That cost is the flip side of the guaranteed coverage workers would gain.

National spending caps and state commission payment rates would apply to Medicare, the public plan, and qualified private plans, restraining what providers are paid. Lower provider payments were the mechanism for the public's lower costs.

industries.industry: Self-employed individuals and small business owners
industries.note: Self-employed people could deduct 100 percent of their health insurance costs (up from 25 percent) indefinitely, and small employers would get a 20 percent premium deduction plus the option to buy public-plan coverage. Small employers also had the public plan as an off-ramp from the mandate.
Removing the wage cap on the hospital insurance tax would raise Medicare payroll taxes on high earners to fund the broader coverage system.
